description:
Found 2026-08-22 wiring op-l3uz's def/sig/refs: RustAnalyzerSession::connect_with_observed spawns a FRESH rust-analyzer and waits out the full index (up to KOVAN_RA_TIMEOUT_SECS, 180s default) on EVERY kovan-cli def/sig/refs invocation, then shuts it down -- no session reuse across separate CLI processes. Fine for a single one-shot query, wasteful for an agent making several in a session.

kopitiam-semantic already ships the right primitive for a long-lived host: AsyncRustAnalyzerSession (crates/kopitiam-semantic/src/async_session.rs) -- spawn_async() returns immediately, state()/is_ready() poll non-blockingly (LspState::Connecting/Ready/Failed), and definition/references/hover/rename/code_actions/apply_code_action all return RequestError::NotReady{state} instead of blocking. This is built for exactly a background-indexing daemon, not a one-shot CLI call.

PROPOSED SHAPE (not yet built, needs a design decision before implementation):
- A 'kovan-cli lsp-daemon' background process hosting one AsyncRustAnalyzerSession per (root, rust-analyzer) pair, listening on a local IPC channel. kovan-cli def/sig/refs (and the not-yet-built rename/code-actions, op-<rename-bead>) become thin clients: check for a live daemon, use it if present, else fall back to today's spawn-per-call path (never a hard dependency on the daemon existing).
- Precedent already dogfooded in this exact workspace: kopi-beans' own 'bn daemon run' (confirmed running via ps aux, 2026-08-22) -- same lazy-spawn / long-lived-background-process shape, so this is not a novel pattern here.
- Lazy spawn on first use, idle-timeout auto-shutdown (e.g. 10-15 min of no requests) so it does not linger forever or need explicit start/stop.
- IPC choice needs a decision: a Unix domain socket is the natural choice on Linux/Termux, but Windows has no Unix sockets (named pipes there) -- this workspace's Android/Windows-portability discipline (CLAUDE.md) means the IPC layer needs a cross-platform answer or an explicit Windows fallback (spawn-per-call, no daemon) before this ships, not an unstated gap.
- Alternative/complementary: kovan-tui, when a human has it open, is ALREADY a long-running process -- it could host the same daemon role, with kovan-cli preferring it if reachable. Doesn't help an agent-only session where nothing keeps kovan-tui open, so the standalone daemon is still needed as the primary path.

notes.author: teddy0@arch-aftershock-rapid-glass-S267454
notes.content: IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-22, revised from the original design during implementation per maintainer direction: NO idle timeout -- the daemon runs until explicitly stopped (kovan-cli lsp-daemon-stop --root <root>), not until N minutes idle. Shipped: crates/kovan/src/commands/lsp_daemon.rs (Unix-domain-socket daemon holding one kopitiam_semantic::AsyncRustAnalyzerSession per workspace root, lazy-spawn-on-first-query via def/sig/refs, newline-delimited JSON request/response, stale-socket recovery on crash). kovan-cli lsp-daemon-serve (hidden, internal) runs it; kovan-cli lsp-daemon-stop (visible) stops it. Windows has no daemon (query() returns None, falls back to spawn-per-call) -- explicit, not silently degraded, per this bead's own original design note. Verified live: cold call ~35-54s (real rust-analyzer index), warm calls 0.1-1s, explicit stop confirmed (process exits, socket removed), stale-socket recovery exercised accidentally (a killed daemon's leftover socket file was correctly detected and replaced). Also found+fixed a real bug during testing: the daemon's original idle-timeout clock started at connection-ACCEPT not connection-FINISH, so a single slow first request (waiting out indexing) could make the daemon look 'idle' the instant it replied -- moot now that idle-timeout was removed entirely, but the fix is preserved in the commit history as a lesson (measure idle from when a request finishes, not when it starts, in any future daemon).

title: kovan-cli: DESIGN -- keep rust-analyzer warm across invocations (daemon, avoid per-call cold-start)

description:
Standing rule added to CLAUDE.md 2026-09-04 (Human interface layer > 'Verifying it: dogfood the API on a small model'). This bead is the harness that makes the rule runnable, plus the first baseline.

WHY. A strong model is the wrong instrument for API usability: when a call is unguessable it reads the Rust and compensates, so the defect never shows up in the result. Measured the same day, an Opus session writing short scripts against our own wheel -- WITH source access and grep -- guessed wrong ten times across six scripts (Sphere's arity, HalfSpaceSense vs bool, k_eff vs k_mean, stage_temperature singular/plural, TrisoRadii/TrisoMaterials wrappers, TrayHydraulics not constructible, ControlDict's thirteen positional args, FvSolution not constructible at all). A model that cannot read the source recovers from none of those, which is exactly why it is the honest probe.

WHAT TO BUILD.
  * A runner that starts a Haiku agent with a FIXED context: the wheel installed and nothing else. No repo, no .pyi, no source. The moment the stubs are in context it is testing something else.
  * A fixed task list spanning the tiers. Proposed: (a) k-eff of a bare HEU sphere; (b) run the pimpleFoam cavity case from a case directory; (c) reconstruct Pu-239 cross sections from an ENDF tape and Doppler-broaden them; (d) sweep reflux ratio on the rigorous MESH column; (e) something needing the low-level CSG types directly.
  * Per task: record round trips to a working script, and log EVERY exception with its message.
  * Aggregate the exception log across tasks, ranked by frequency. That ranked list is the backlog, and it is the deliverable -- same technique as outram-park/codegen/blocked.md one level up, which is what surfaced the generic-alias bug nobody had suspected.

TAKE THE BASELINE BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING. The error-message and constructor work already discussed (self-describing enum errors, did-you-mean on attributes, Geometry::sphere/slab/box constructors, making mc_keff_of_actinide_sphere compose over run_keff_csg) should be measured against this baseline, not asserted.

NOT IN SCOPE. This measures discoverability, not physics. A script can run and be nonsense; the V&V tests remain the only check on correctness. A failure unique to the small model is likely its own priors rather than our API -- the tell is whether a different model trips on the same call.

notes.author: teddy0@snrsi-arch-desktop
notes.content:
SCOPE EXTENDED 2026-09-04 — two additions.

1. RUST-SIDE CUSTOM DIAGNOSTICS, same principle one layer down.

A confusing trait-bound error is the compiler's version of an undiscoverable API. `#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]` is stable since Rust 1.78 and works on our 1.98 toolchain — verified here:

    #[diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
        message = "`{Self}` is not a valid solver state",
        label = "needs an OdeSystem",
        note = "construct one with `MySystem::new(..)`"
    )]
    trait OdeSystem {}

produces `error[E0277]: `u32` is not a valid solver state` with our label and note, in place of the default "the trait bound is not satisfied". `#[diagnostic::do_not_recommend]` (stable 1.85) suppresses a blanket impl the compiler would otherwise suggest unhelpfully.

The workspace has 65 public traits and, as of today, zero carry either attribute. Any trait whose bound a caller can plausibly fail should. Work item: audit the 65, annotate the ones with non-obvious bounds, starting with those a downstream crate actually names in a generic signature.

BE CLEAR ABOUT WHO THIS SERVES. on_unimplemented helps RUST callers and does nothing whatsoever for a Python user holding the wheel — the compiler is not in their loop. The Python-side equivalent is the pyo3 runtime error: an enum error that names its constructors, a wrong-attribute error that suggests the right one. Same design idea, two different layers, and the harness only measures the second. Do not conflate them or count one as progress on the other.

2. LITERATURE. The method has a lineage worth citing rather than reinventing.

  * API usability evaluation is a mature field — a systematic mapping covers 47 primary studies (Rauf et al. 2019, Comput. Sci. Rev.). The dominant instrument is the Cognitive Dimensions Framework questionnaire (Wijayarathna et al. 2017/2019; Piccioni et al. 2013, ESEM, 120 citations). The CD questionnaire is a ready-made structure for this bead's task list — use it rather than inventing categories.
  * Piccioni et al. found the top empirical issues to be 'the difficulty of finding good names for API features and of discovering relations between API types'. That is exactly what the Opus session hit here (two distinct Sphere types; having to discover that RegionToken relates to HalfSpaceSense), which is evidence the failures are the field's known dominant modes rather than anything exotic.
  * LLM-as-evaluator is very new: 'Lessons from API Usability Analyses Using an LLM' (John et al., CHI 2026 EA) uses a custom GPT to APPLY the CD framework on the designer's behalf — the model is the analyst, not the subject.
  * Nearest agentic work: 'ADK Arena: Evaluating Agent Development Kits via LLM-as-a-Developer' (arXiv 2606.05548); 'Diagnosing Knowledge Gaps in LLM Tool Use: An Agentic Benchmark for Novel API Acquisition' (2606.03657); 'ZhuLong: Execution-Grounded LLM Agent for EDA Scripting with Offline API Self-Exploration' (2608.07925).
  * NOT FOUND in two searches: the deliberate capability downgrade as the measurement principle — choosing a weaker model BECAUSE a stronger one masks the defect by reading source — with the ranked exception log as the defect backlog. Stated as not-found, not as novel; two searches is not a systematic review.

The framing that makes it defensible: usability testing requires representative users, not experts. Opus with grep is the expert who routes around the defect; Haiku with only the wheel is the representative user. The principle is old, the observation that model capability IS the expert/novice axis is the new part.

title: Build the Haiku API-dogfooding harness and take a baseline

description:
faer 0.24's DEFAULT feature set includes 'rayon', which pulls dep:spindle -> atomic-wait, and atomic-wait has no wasm32 backend ('cannot find module or crate platform'). Affects bedok and outram-blender.

faer 0.24.4 features: default = [std, rayon, sparse-linalg, rand, npy]. The wasm-safe subset is roughly [std, sparse-linalg, linalg] — verify 'rand' and 'npy' individually, npy pulls npyz (file I/O) and rand pulls the rand stack which has its own wasm story.

faer is a ROOT [workspace.dependencies] entry (Cargo.toml:120, currently bare 'faer = "0.24"'), so per the workspace dependency policy the version lives there. Suggested shape: set default-features=false plus the common feature set in the root table, then let members that want rayon add it back per-target:

  [target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dependencies]
  faer = { workspace = true, features = ["rayon"] }
  [target.'cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")'.dependencies]
  faer = { workspace = true }

Confirm outram-foam-basic-lib (which also uses faer) is unaffected — it currently PASSES the wasm check, so check why before changing the shared entry and accidentally regressing it.

Acceptance: bedok and outram-blender pass the wasm --lib check; native builds keep rayon-accelerated faer; no regression in outram-foam-basic-lib or Android.

notes.author: teddy0@snrsi-arch-desktop
notes.content:
CANCELLED — EXCLUDED by maintainer decision, 2026-09-04: bedok and outram-blender are out of scope for wasm.

Both were failing on faer's default feature set (faer 0.24 default includes 'rayon', which pulls dep:spindle -> atomic-wait, and atomic-wait has no wasm32 backend). The fix was understood and small — declare faer with default-features=false and re-add 'rayon' per-target — but the crates are not wanted as wasm targets, so the change is not worth making.

Recorded for whoever revisits: the root [workspace.dependencies] faer entry stays as bare 'faer = "0.24"'. This bead's plan still applies unchanged if a wasm target is ever wanted. Note outram-foam-basic-lib also uses faer and currently PASSES the wasm check — check why before touching the shared entry, so a fix for these two does not regress that one.

Both crates go on the exclusion list in the class-F gate (op-okqo.6) with this reason, so they are visibly excluded rather than silently absent.
